title: Why 99% of LinkedIn Posts Suck (Do This Instead) | Alec Paul
speakers_and_attribution: Adam Robinson is a participant alongside guest LinkedIn strategist Alec Paul and a moderating co-host identified contextually as Pete; Pete's surname is not established. John, introduced with an unclear surname as a Sales Table representative, delivers the opening product pitch. Captions are not diarized, so speaker assignments rely on conversational context. Diana Ross, Sam Jacobs, and Tom Hunt are discussed but do not speak. The opening contains preview excerpts, and the final cold-email excerpt has uncertain attribution and ends mid-sentence.
summary: The workshop examines founder-led LinkedIn marketing through audience specificity, credible hooks, sustained practice, reusable content, storytelling, and audience relationships. Adam describes his writing workflow, a year before LinkedIn meaningfully worked, earlier struggles with video advertising, and his shift toward sharing the emotional experience of building RB2B. Alec supplies most of the tactical guidance and emphasizes quality, consistency, and treating business experience as source material. Live post critiques and the final Q&A cover readability, sales framing, engagement giveaways, scheduling, and platform dependence. Business and audience figures are spoken self-reports or secondhand examples, with several missing units or unclear periods. The title's 99% claim is not substantiated in the discussion.

key_learnings.claim: Alec's role in Adam's content operation includes idea generation, hook refinement, performance review, and calendar planning; Adam says Alec does not write the posts for him.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson, with Alec Paul confirming the writing distinction
key_learnings.caveat: Describes this working relationship at the time of recording; it does not establish authorship practices for every other format or period.

key_learnings.claim: Alec argues that posts need a specific audience, a specific pain, and a distinct perspective before technical improvements to hooks or storytelling can help much.
key_learnings.speaker: Alec Paul
key_learnings.caveat: Practitioner advice, not a measured universal rule.

key_learnings.claim: For beginners, Alec recommends developing the hook before investing in a full post. He allows that an experienced writer can sometimes draft a strong idea first and discover its hook afterward.
key_learnings.speaker: Alec Paul
key_learnings.caveat: The discussion explicitly includes an exception to a strict hook-first workflow.

key_learnings.claim: Adam captures ideas during the week, works through hooks with Alec, and keeps more developed options than he needs for each writing session so he can move past ideas that do not inspire him.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: His desired writing setup is mixed with descriptions of current practice; the number of prepared options is a target.

key_learnings.claim: Adam treats each post as an introduction to a fresh audience: the hook and profile description should establish relevant credibility without assuming readers know his previous content.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: Adam explicitly credits Alec for much of this framework. The example about Diana's sales experience is not Adam's own achievement.

key_learnings.claim: Adam favors authentic, defensible contrarian positions that have a strong opposing side. He uses his broad advocacy of bootstrapping as an example while acknowledging that bootstrapping is not universally appropriate.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: He is explaining a social-content tactic and explicitly qualifies the literal universality of his stance.

key_learnings.claim: Adam recommends concrete numbers in hooks and suggests earning credibility by gathering useful information from others when a writer lacks a large personal business outcome.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: His example about interviewing ten startups on cold email in 2025 is a proposed post concept, not a reported research project.

key_learnings.claim: Alec says a hook should create a reason to expand the post. That can come from an explicit tease or from a situation whose unresolved outcome naturally creates curiosity.
key_learnings.speaker: Alec Paul
key_learnings.caveat: The startup-failure story used as an example is a secondhand recollection of someone else's post.

key_learnings.claim: Pete uses the team's account of cutting demand-generation spending while subsequently growing as an example of a counterintuitive business decision that creates a compelling content premise.
key_learnings.speaker: Pete, co-host
key_learnings.caveat: He paraphrases an earlier post approximately. The sequence does not establish that the spending cuts caused growth.

key_learnings.claim: Alec encourages founders to document real building, experiments, customer conversations, and learning. He describes the creator's role as reporting on business experience and says this does not require disclosing all revenue or churn figures.
key_learnings.speaker: Alec Paul
key_learnings.caveat: This is Alec's proposed approach, not an approved mission statement for Adam. One sentence about customer problems is garbled.

key_learnings.claim: Adam says LinkedIn initially felt directionless despite his ability to explain his product and marketing decisions. After roughly a year, he understood his writing choices much better, although strong-looking posts still sometimes failed.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: Meaningful success is subjectively defined. His failed John Mackey post is a single example, not evidence about the broader appeal of criticism of VC.

key_learnings.claim: Alec treats content performance as feedback that requires a hypothesis and another test. He advises against explaining every failure through the algorithm while acknowledging outages and changing distribution behavior.
key_learnings.speaker: Alec Paul
key_learnings.caveat: His claim that the audience is right is a working heuristic; the conversation also recognizes platform effects.

key_learnings.claim: Alec would retry a promising failed post with a different hook or without its video. He frames accumulated posts as reusable intellectual property that can be remixed, republished, and potentially turned into ads.
key_learnings.speaker: Alec Paul
key_learnings.caveat: The proposed retry is not confirmed as completed. Some brief interjections in this exchange may be Adam's.

key_learnings.claim: Alec balances practice volume against quality: beginners need repetitions, but rushing posts to satisfy an arbitrary calendar can undermine the exceptional posts that drive growth.
key_learnings.speaker: Alec Paul
key_learnings.caveat: He explicitly says the quality-versus-quantity balance has changed over time. His engagement comparisons are illustrative, not controlled results.

key_learnings.claim: Pete argues that repeated mediocre content trains an audience to ignore future work, using a musician's release quality to explain why a reputation for low-value output is costly across channels.
key_learnings.speaker: Pete, co-host
key_learnings.caveat: An analogy rather than empirical evidence about publishing frequency.

key_learnings.claim: Alec recommends giving useful content before asking for action, especially while building an audience. He favors strategic selling periods over constant promotional requests and describes RB2B's launch as a period of heavier promotion.
key_learnings.speaker: Alec Paul
key_learnings.caveat: He does not prohibit outbound links or selling. The promotional balance depends on the stage and campaign.

key_learnings.claim: Adam believes repeated useful posts can make readers curious enough to visit his business without a sales CTA in every post. He considers the profile-level website button an important conversion path.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: His assertion that all RB2B traffic comes from LinkedIn is an unverified attribution claim, recorded separately in the metric ledger.

key_learnings.claim: Alec says RB2B became a recurring character in Adam's content through launches, setbacks, and learning, providing a natural way to generate company interest without making every post an explicit product pitch.
key_learnings.speaker: Alec Paul
key_learnings.caveat: Alec notes that this approach depends on whom the company sells to and will not fit every business.

key_learnings.claim: Adam says he progressed from templates and fact-heavy updates toward stories about frustration and the emotional experience of being stuck, which he considers more relatable and engaging.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: This describes his own evolution and belief about effectiveness; no comparative performance figures are supplied.

key_learnings.claim: Adam frames founder community value as both education and companionship through difficult experiences. He says shared experience addresses loneliness he personally felt until relatively recently.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: His final autobiographical sentence is interrupted. The educational value multiple is an aspiration, not a measured customer outcome.

key_learnings.claim: In the inbound-machine post critique, Alec asks the writer to identify the audience, explain who achieved the result, and include relevant constraints in the opening instead of repeating broad inbound language.
key_learnings.speaker: Alec Paul
key_learnings.caveat: The displayed post is not fully transcribed, so the assessment cannot be independently reconstructed from captions alone.

key_learnings.claim: Alec would lead a product-related post with useful detail about how an outcome was achieved, then introduce the product or demo near the end. He believes an obvious demo pitch can make readers disengage too early.
key_learnings.speaker: Alec Paul
key_learnings.caveat: Advice about sequencing educational and promotional content; he allows that a sufficiently compelling demo video may work.

key_learnings.claim: The communication-post critique recommends creating stakes through a concrete negative consequence of poor communication and reducing the reading burden caused by a text-heavy image accompanying substantial post text.
key_learnings.speaker: Alec Paul, likely; one intervening critique may be another participant
key_learnings.caveat: Speaker transitions are unclear and the full visual example is unavailable.

key_learnings.claim: Alec considers a strong premise insufficient when presentation creates friction. He recommends breaking dense paragraphs into readable sections, particularly for mobile, and says link previews appear to underperform plain links in his experience.
key_learnings.speaker: Alec Paul
key_learnings.caveat: The link-preview penalty is an observational platform claim; Alec explicitly says he does not know why it happens.

key_learnings.claim: Alec says comment-to-receive-asset posts can increase reach, followers, and inbound interest, but may attract people outside the ICP and create brand costs. He recommends considering whether the tactic fits the brand.
key_learnings.speaker: Alec Paul
key_learnings.caveat: He distinguishes distribution gains from attracting likely buyers and does not claim permanent effectiveness.

key_learnings.claim: Alec identifies fulfillment as a major weakness of comment-based giveaways: creators often fail to deliver, and a large response can exceed their ability to message people. Successful engagement therefore creates an operational obligation.
key_learnings.speaker: Alec Paul
key_learnings.caveat: His delivery-rate estimate and claims about messaging limits are anecdotal and unverified. This is not a recommendation to scrape or automate.

key_learnings.claim: Alec recommends a sustainable commitment measured in years, comparing posting to exercise. He warns that stopping for months can erase momentum and that seven-day publishing schedules may create burnout.
key_learnings.speaker: Alec Paul
key_learnings.caveat: A planning framework, not a guaranteed time to business results or a universal prohibition on daily posting.

key_learnings.claim: For more advanced content, Alec recommends developing recurring narratives with recognizable tensions and language. He describes Adam's themes around bootstrapping, VC, building in public, and sales approaches as partly planned and partly discovered through audience response.
key_learnings.speaker: Alec Paul
key_learnings.caveat: Alec's interpretation of the content program; some named themes are garbled in captions and do not establish Adam's complete beliefs.

key_learnings.claim: Adam explains that apparent confidence came after earlier awkward attempts at video advertising, on-camera coaching, and impostor feelings. He presents visible skill as the result of a much longer learning history.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: His earlier SaaS is unnamed; the unsuccessful early experiments should not be conflated with the successful 2020 campaign.

key_learnings.claim: Alec favors LinkedIn's native scheduler and avoids third-party automation because he sees account continuity as important to the long-term value of a founder audience. He reports that native scheduling has not appeared to reduce distribution.
key_learnings.speaker: Alec Paul
key_learnings.caveat: Source-period advice, not a verified account of current platform rules. He admits lingering attachment to old live-posting beliefs.

key_learnings.claim: Alec suggests that live posting can look stronger because the author is present to engage. He identifies comments, connections, and conversations as additional distribution levers while recognizing executives have limited time.
key_learnings.speaker: Alec Paul
key_learnings.caveat: Includes unverified claims about platform behavior, particularly DM conversations influencing feed exposure.

key_learnings.claim: When engagement declines, Adam recommends improving hooks and content regardless of the suspected cause. Alec agrees and acknowledges that the platform controls distribution and that badge-related decline reports lack a clear explanation.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson, followed by Alec Paul
key_learnings.caveat: Adam's recommendation ends around 00:49:36; platform-dependence and badge comments are Alec's. No shadowban or badge penalty is established.

key_learnings.claim: In the closing discussion, Alec suggests broad workplace topics can attract unusually large LinkedIn engagement, while the participants speculate about additional tactics behind Tom Hunt's results.
key_learnings.speaker: Alec Paul, with host interjections
key_learnings.caveat: The participants do not establish what caused Hunt's performance; joking speculation is not evidence of misconduct.

key_learnings.claim: The final excerpt argues that inbox placement precedes subject-line optimization and uses a familiar sender as an example of why someone may open an email regardless of its subject.
key_learnings.speaker: Unidentified speaker in closing excerpt
key_learnings.caveat: Appears to be a separate closing clip, with a garbled example and an unfinished explanation of the next priority. It should not be assigned to Adam.

tensions_and_corrections: The title's claim that 99% of posts are poor is not substantiated by spoken evidence and should not become a wiki statistic.
Adam explicitly qualifies his broad pro-bootstrapping rhetoric: he knows it is not universally applicable and discusses its ability to provoke debate.
Hook-first advice has an explicit exception for experienced writers who can discover the hook during drafting. Later critiques also show that readability and presentation matter alongside the hook.

Alec favors quality over rushed frequency while also emphasizing repetition and consistency. These positions support a sustainable practice schedule, not either maximal volume or occasional perfectionism.

Alec's six-to-twelve-month early-investment horizon and later twelve-to-twenty-four-month commitment describe different planning frames. Neither is a guaranteed time to results; Adam's one-year experience is separately self-reported.
Adam's 'first social post' in fall 2022 coexists with a successful 2020 Facebook ad campaign and earlier video experiments because he distinguishes posting from advertising.

The $25 million ARR reference and RB2B's unspecified '5 million' milestone cannot be reconciled into a growth series: company identity is missing for the former and the unit is missing for the latter.

The marketing example alternates between cutting demand-generation channels, cutting all marketing channels, and stopping ad spend, while the workshop itself is described as brand marketing. It does not establish that all marketing activity ended.
The reported $100,000 monthly savings and approximately 15% growth are Pete's approximate recollection of a post. The growth measure and causal mechanism are not established.

Diana's 20,000-follower figure and the garbled comparison with Adam do not establish Adam's follower total. Her two zero-to-$10 million ARR journeys are her attributed experience, not Adam's sole-sales achievement.
The post-library count shifts verbally between hundreds and thousands; preserve it as imprecise rather than selecting a precise total.

Alec frames poor performance as audience feedback but also acknowledges platform changes, outages, unexplained slumps, and uncertain badge effects. Performance is not presented consistently as a pure measure of content quality.

Alec says native scheduling seems acceptable while admitting that he still sometimes posts live because of old beliefs. His explanation involving engagement is observational, not a controlled comparison.
Comment-gated assets can produce impressive engagement while attracting nonbuyers and creating unfulfilled promises. The stated reach benefits do not establish qualified pipeline or sales conversion.

The course was announced as public, then attendees reported it locked; later the co-host said a free account was needed and some attendees confirmed access. Any promise to close access 'tomorrow' is source-relative and does not establish present availability.
Adam's joke about his software products having poor retention supplies no churn metric, cohort, or period. It should not be entered as quantified evidence of product performance.
The final cold-email passage is an incomplete, possibly separate promotional excerpt. Its speaker and unfinished hierarchy of email priorities remain unknown.
